# Pāsādika Sutta (DN 29 (PTS DN iii 117))
**ID:** DN 29 (PTS DN iii 117)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Pāsādika Sutta* (DN 29) is a major discourse delivered by the Buddha while dwelling among the Sakyans, prompted by the recent death of Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta at Pāvā and the ensuing sectarian fragmentation and quarreling among his Jain followers [SuttaCentral; Gethin 2001; Norman 1983]. When the novice Cunda reports these schismatic events to Ānanda, both approach the Buddha, who addresses Cunda on the contrast between an ill-proclaimed doctrine and a well-expounded dispensation [Gethin 2001; Freedman 1977]. The Buddha explains that the completeness of his holy life is reflected in the spiritual accomplishment of the fourfold assembly, notably requiring the order of nuns [Anālayo 2016]. He also addresses the nature of the Tathāgata's knowledge of the past and future [Pandey 1972]. To preserve the Dhamma and avoid future discord after his passing, the Buddha exhorts the community to recite the teachings in harmony, comparing meaning to meaning and phrasing to phrasing, specifically centering on the factors leading to awakening [SuttaCentral; Peoples 2013; Gethin 2001]. The discourse concludes with the elder Upavāna fanning the Buddha [Freedman 1977].
Scholars have noted that the text shares its historical setting and opening narrative with the *Sāmagāma Sutta* (MN 104)—where the Buddha addresses Ānanda rather than Cunda—as well as the *Saṅgīti Sutta* (DN 33) [Gethin 2001; Freedman 1977; Norman 1983]. SuttaCentral identifies full parallels in the Chinese *Dīrgha Āgama* (DĀ 17), Sanskrit manuscript fragments (SHT sutta 39 and SF 58), MN 76, and AN 9.7–8 [SuttaCentral]. Computational analysis via DharmaNexus confirms substantial text reuse across the canon, demonstrating prominent overlap with the *Mahāparinibbāna Sutta* (DN 16), an opening sequence shared almost verbatim with the *Saṅgīti Sutta* (DN 33), and numerous passages shared with AN 10, AN 4, and SN 47, as well as alignments with the Chinese *Dīrgha Āgama* and the Sanskrit *Saṅgītisūtra* [DharmaNexus].
